passage: I'm Jagdish, and I teach Class 5. Let me describe Naveen, because the staffroom keeps asking. He finishes the maths worksheet in ten minutes. Then he asks things like, "Sir, why is zero even?" or "Who decided a week has seven days?" By minute fifteen he's balancing his bottle on his head and the back row is laughing. At first I gave him two more worksheets. He did them in eight minutes and the bottle came out again. So last week I tried something else. I gave him one open question: "Find three ways to prove zero is even, and one way someone might argue it isn't." He worked for the whole period, then asked to present it. The bottle stayed in his bag. His questions now go up on a board by the window.

qa.q: What question did Jagdish give Naveen last week?
qa.a: Find three ways to prove zero is even, and one way someone might argue it isn't.

qa.q: How does Jagdish seem to feel about Naveen's questions by the end?
qa.a: He seems encouraged by them, since one open question kept Naveen working the whole period, so he now puts Naveen's questions on a board by the window.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Extra worksheets only added more of the same; one deeper, open question kept Naveen interested for the whole period.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel once his questions go up on the board?
qa.a: Naveen may feel his curiosity is valued rather than a nuisance, which is why he now works for the whole period.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: Tuesday. Dhruv, eleven, finished the plant worksheet first, then asked Avni Ma'am, "But why don't plants fall over when they grow toward the light?" She said, "Not now, Dhruv," and handed him another worksheet. He folded it into a paper plane and flew it across the room. Thursday. Avni had thought about it. When Dhruv finished early, she said, "Your question from Tuesday. Want to test it?" She gave him a bean seedling, a shoebox and a torch. He spent the lesson cutting a window in the box. The following Monday. Dhruv presented his bent seedling to the class, explaining every step. When Suhail asked a question, Dhruv said, "Good question. I don't know yet." Avni noticed no paper planes all week.

qa.q: What did Avni give Dhruv on Thursday?
qa.a: A bean seedling, a shoebox and a torch.

qa.q: How does Avni seem to feel about Dhruv's question after thinking it over?
qa.a: She seems to regret brushing it off and now respects his curiosity, offering him an experiment to test it instead of another worksheet.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Avni's approach?
qa.a: She took his earlier question seriously and gave him a deeper experiment instead of an extra worksheet.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel presenting his bent seedling to the class?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt proud and taken seriously, confident enough to tell Suhail, 'I don't know yet.'

grounding: It shows a teacher who notices a bright pupil finishing early, asking probing questions and disrupting, and who keeps his interest alive with depth, not extra workload.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: "Varun, you're frustrated with that boy who keeps disrupting your class? Let me tell you about Mukul, my old student. He finished every sum before I'd written the last one on the board. Then he'd ask, 'Ma'am, if there are infinite stars, why is the sky dark?' I didn't know! Then he'd throw paper balls at the fan. At first I gave him two extra worksheets. He threw more paper balls. So one day I said, 'Mukul, that sky question is a real puzzle. Find out, and teach it to us on Friday.' He spent the week in the library. On Friday he taught us with a torch and a steel plate. No paper balls. More sums was the mistake; a bigger question was the answer." Sunaina poured the tea.

qa.q: What did Mukul use when he taught the class on Friday?
qa.a: He used a torch and a steel plate.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Mukul asked his star question?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little stumped, since she didn't know the answer, but she came to respect the question.

qa.q: What choice inside the story changed Mukul's behaviour?
qa.a: Sunaina stopped giving extra worksheets and instead asked him to research his own question and teach it, giving depth instead of more work.

qa.q: How might Mukul have felt when asked to teach the class?
qa.a: He probably felt respected and excited, because his question was taken seriously and he had a real challenge.

passage: With the other teacher absent, Tenzin had two classes squeezed into one room, sixty-eight children, and the fans rattling. Wasim, ten, finished the fractions task in three minutes. "Sir, why can't you divide by zero? What actually happens?" Before Tenzin could answer, Wasim was drumming on the desk, and the back row joined in. Tenzin's first thought was to hand him another page of fractions. Instead he crouched by the desk. "Good question. Here's a bigger one. How would you split sixty-eight children into fair teams for the quiz? Show me three ways." Wasim grabbed his notebook. The drumming stopped. Ten minutes later he had four ways, and a note: "Divide by zero is like splitting sweets among no children. Ask me later."

qa.q: How many children were in the room?
qa.a: There were sixty-eight children in the room.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling as the drumming spread?
qa.a: He was likely stressed and tempted to hand Wasim more fractions, with a crowded, noisy room to control.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin's choice work better than extra worksheets?
qa.a: He respected Wasim's question and gave him a deeper, real problem to solve, which kept Wasim interested instead of bored.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt when Tenzin called his question good?
qa.a: Wasim probably felt valued and eager, which is why he grabbed his notebook and stopped drumming.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a pupil who finishes early, asks probing questions and disrupts, and responding with depth and respect instead of more work, despite a crowded room.

subtype: Teacher noticing a restless bright child [Observer]
passage: In her Delhi classroom, Gurpreet Ma'am watched Eshaan, eight, finish the clock worksheet first again. "Ma'am, who decided a minute has sixty seconds? Why not a hundred?" She smiled, said "Good question, later," and gave him another worksheet. Within minutes he was flicking erasers at the fan. Gurpreet sighed and wondered if she had got it wrong. At break she sat with him and wrote his question on a card. "Your job this week: find out who first counted in sixties. Tell the class on Friday." Eshaan's eyes went wide. On Friday he explained, with drawings, how people long ago counted in sixties on their finger joints. The erasers stayed in his pencil box all week.

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask about minutes?
qa.a: He asked who decided a minute has sixty seconds, and why not a hundred.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when Eshaan started flicking erasers?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and doubtful, sighing and wondering whether her extra worksheet had been the wrong move.

qa.q: What worked better than giving Eshaan another worksheet?
qa.a: Taking his question seriously and turning it into a research task he could share with the class, which added depth, not workload.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt when given the research card?
qa.a: He probably felt excited and taken seriously; his eyes went wide and he stopped flicking erasers.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a bright pupil who finishes early, asks probing questions and disrupts, and finding that depth and respect for questions work better than extra work.

passage:
"Done, Ma'am."
"Mohit, I gave those sums four minutes ago."
"They were easy. Ma'am, why can't you divide by zero? What would happen?"
Kiran Ma'am paused. "Good question. Let's talk after—"
But by the time she had checked three notebooks, Mohit was flicking paper balls at Arjun and humming.
After class, Kiran Ma'am called him over. "Mohit, you're disturbing others."
"I'm bored, Ma'am. Should I just do more sums?"
"No. More sums won't help you. Here's something harder. Find three different ways to explain why dividing by zero doesn't work. You can use drawings, stories, anything. Show me on Friday."
Mohit's eyes widened. "Anything?"
"Anything. And bring me your next question too. I like your questions."
On Friday he brought four explanations and a new question about infinity.

qa.q: How many explanations did Mohit bring on Friday?
qa.a: He brought four explanations and a new question about infinity.

qa.q: What was Kiran Ma'am feeling when she told Mohit she liked his questions?
qa.a: She felt genuine interest and admiration for his curious mind, even though his disruption had annoyed her.

qa.q: Why did Kiran Ma'am's task work better than extra sums?
qa.a: It gave Mohit deeper, open-ended thinking instead of more of the same work, and respected his questions, so his interest stayed alive.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when told he could use anything to explain?
qa.a: He likely felt excited and valued, as if his curiosity was finally welcome in class.
